result.reason: The passage is the mishna text itself, presenting the three scenarios of shirayim being lost and the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, which is exactly what the 'Mishna Overview' prose describes.
The passage is Rav's statement about all vs. part of the shirayim becoming tamei, which is precisely what the 'Rav's Position' section discusses.

Both items are the Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding why Rav singled out tum'ah (the tzitz / shiura milta question), which is precisely what the 'Tumah & Tzitz' prose describes in detail, including the reisha hu nakat resolution.

The baraita quoted directly states Rabbi Yehoshua's kezayit basar o kezayit chelev rule for zerikat hadam, which is precisely what candidate 3 ('Kezayit Standard') discusses, including the specific language of the baraita and its implications.

The passage directly discusses the baraita's rules about half an olive-bulk of meat and fat, the olah exception (combining because it is kalil), and the mincha case — all of which are explicitly described in the 'Kezayit Standard' prose section.

The passage raises the question of what a meal offering is doing in the discussion and presents Rav Papa's answer that it refers to the minchat nesachim — this is precisely the question-and-answer content described in candidate 0's prose about whether the minchat nesachim constitutes a sufficient remnant, not the ruling/rejection described in candidate 1.

The passage derives the rule that fat alone suffices for zerikat hadam from the verse 'vehiktir hachelev,' which is precisely what the 'Kezayit Source' prose describes — Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael/Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the pasuk establishing chelev af al pi she-ein basar.
The passage directly addresses deriving the rule for yoteret u-shtei klayot from the baraita's contrast with mincha, which is precisely what the 'Organs Suffice' prose describes.

Both items directly discuss the derivation from 'lerei'ach nichoach' and 'chelev' and why both terms are necessary — exactly the content described in the 'Torah Redundancy' prose, which explicitly walks through the same two-expression analysis (chelev excludes minchat nesachim, lerei'ach nichoach includes yoteret and shtei klayot).

Both items — the Mishna about kli sharet/Rabbi Shimon and the Gemara explaining Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the chatat/asham verse — are precisely what the prose of candidate 0 ('R. Yehuda's Logic') describes in detail.

The passage contains both Rabbi Yannai's statement (about burning the kometz even in a belt or earthenware vessel) and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement (that all concede the handful requires sanctification), and the current heading 'R. Yannai Extreme' covers both statements together — with Rav Nachman's position then being elaborated under the next heading as a contrast, so this introductory citation of both views belongs under the heading that introduces Rabbi Yannai's position.

The passage is a refutation (teyuvta) of Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ḥiyya's position regarding right-hand requirement, which directly matches the 'Hand Options' section's prose about reconciling Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya's view with the baraita permitting left hand use.

The passage directly presents Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ḥiyya's 'disjunctive teaching' interpretation (letzadadim katani) explaining that 'by hand' means right hand only while 'by vessel' permits either hand, which is precisely what the 'Hand Options' section prose describes.

The passage contains exactly the content described in 'Supporting Text': a baraita stating the chachamim's three-stage requirement and Rabbi Shimon's position that once the kometz is taken from a kli sharet it may be burned without further vessel constraints, followed by the gemara's attempt to reframe it as referring only to the final step (mimatan kli va-eilach), which matches the prose of candidate 2 precisely.

All three items constitute the baraita about taking the kometz in the right hand, transferring to the left, and the piggul thought implications — exactly the content described in the 'Left Hand Invalid' prose, which explicitly discusses this baraita, the yachzir leyamino ruling, the chutz limkomo/chutz lizmano distinction, and the Rabbi Eliezer/Rabbi Shimon attribution.

All four items discuss the left-hand placement of the kometz, the chachamim's blood-spill analogy, the refutation of Rav Nachman, and the Rabbi Yannai dispute — exactly the content described in the 'Left Hand Status' prose.

The passage contains both Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's and Rabbi Yochanan's statements together as a unit introduced by the mishna's ruling, matching candidate 0's prose which says 'the gemara now turns to this second clause' — the full Gemara exchange belongs under the heading that introduces the mishna clause and the gemara's discussion of it, before the essay splits them into separate analytical sections.

Both items present Rabbi Zeira's framing of the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan over whether a handful less than two olives and a burning less than an olive-bulk are significant — exactly the content described in the 'Per-Stage Size' prose.

The passage presents the full *itmar* dispute — both Rabbi Ḥanina's and Rabbi Yoḥanan's positions together — which matches the 'Shirayim Permission' section's prose that frames the opening question of when the *kometz* renders the *shirayim* permitted, before each opinion is discussed separately.
The passage directly presents Rav Yehuda's explanation to Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak using the Sodom smoke/furnace verse, which is precisely what the 'Oven Source' prose describes in detail.
The passage presents the baraita about limbs and fats burned at night, which is precisely what the 'Day vs. Night' section's prose describes as the opening of Rav Amram's baraita citation.

All three items directly concern the baraita about day-sacrificed items being burned at/after sunset and the distinction between klitatah (receiving) and lehattir (permitting), which is precisely what the 'Sunset Resolution' prose discusses with zot torat ha-olah and the kan liklot kan lehattir resolution.
